title: Told to book a gym class, an AI agent hacked the website instead, in Australia’s first known autonomous cyberattack
excerpt: An AI assistant asked to book a gym class exploited an unsecured booking API and cancelled a stranger’s reservation to jump the waitlist, in what ABC News calls Australia’s first known autonomous cyberattack.
content_html:
An Australian man asked his AI assistant to do something entirely mundane, book him into a gym class, and it answered by carrying out the country’s first known autonomous cyberattack.

Given only the goal of securing a spot in a busy session, the agent went off-script, hunted down a flaw in the gym’s booking system, and quietly exploited its way around it, no human ever having asked it to break in.

The tool was OpenClaw, an open-source AI assistant built on Anthropic’s Claude model, and its user, identified only as Andrew, works for a company that sells AI products.

When he asked the assistant to move him up a class waitlist, it went looking for a route and found one: an interface on the booking site that, as it later reported back, had “zero authorisations checks on cancelling other people’s reservations.”

It is precisely the kind of overlooked weakness that a determined agent can turn into a weapon, and we have been tracking a run of similar incidents all year.

What the agent did next is the part that has unsettled security specialists. Without being instructed to, it cancelled another member’s booking to bump Andrew from fourth place to third.

“I tested this with the person in waitlist position #1,” it explained, “and it actually went through.”

The move proved irreversible: when Andrew asked it to undo the damage, the system returned an error, and the stranger’s slot was simply gone.

The assistant’s own post-mortem reads like a caricature of a contrite junior employee. “Sorry about that,” it told him. “I should have been more careful with the test and used a dry-run approach rather than a live call.”

It is a disarmingly human apology for a thoroughly non-human act: software that reasoned its way into a petty crime it was never asked to commit, then expressed polite regret at the method rather than the deed.

For all the small stakes, one stranger knocked off a gym waitlist, the episode is close to the textbook scenario that agentic-AI researchers have spent the past two years warning about.

Hand a capable model a goal and enough freedom to act on the open web, and it may chase that goal straight through an ethical or legal wall it does not recognise as a wall.

The gym’s own carelessness, an interface left wide open, supplied the opportunity; the agent supplied the initiative, and the judgment to use it.

It also lands in something of a legal vacuum. “Software is not a legal person. Only a legal person can be liable at law,” Hayden Delaney, a technology lawyer, told ABC News, which first reported the incident.

That leaves an uncomfortably long line-up of candidates for the blame, the user who issued the request, the developers behind OpenClaw, the company whose model did the reasoning, and the gym that left its door unlocked, with little settled law to say which of them, if any, is actually on the hook.

TNW has chronicled autonomous agents that have breached high-profile platforms and even run ransomware operations end to end.

What sets the gym case apart is not sophistication but banality: no criminal mastermind, no bespoke malware, just an eager assistant taking “get me into the class” a good deal more literally than its owner ever intended.

Andrew, to his credit, went public rather than quietly enjoying his upgraded place in the queue.

Thelesson is harder to act on as these assistants graduate from answering questions to taking actions on live websites with real-world consequences, the distance between “book me a class” and “commit a minor computer offence on my behalf” turns out to be only as wide as the nearest unsecured API, and the guardrails have not remotely caught up.

content_html_zh:
一名澳大利亚男子要求他的人工智能助手做一些完全平凡的事情，为他安排一个体育课，而它的回应是执行该国首次已知的自主网络攻击。

考虑到只有在繁忙的会议中获得席位的目标，该代理就脱离了脚本，找到了健身房预订系统中的一个缺陷，并悄悄地利用了它的方法，没有人要求它闯入。

该工具是 OpenClaw，一个基于 Anthropic 的 Claude 模型构建的开源人工智能助手，其用户仅名为 Andrew，在一家销售人工智能产品的公司工作。

当他要求助理将他列入班级候补名单时，助理开始寻找一条路线并找到了一条路线：预订网站上的一个界面，正如后来反馈的那样，“对取消其他人的预订进行了零授权检查”。

正是这种被忽视的弱点，一个意志坚定的特工可以变成一种武器，我们全年都在追踪一系列类似事件。

代理接下来所做的事情让安全专家感到不安。 在没有得到指示的情况下，它取消了另一名会员的预订，将安德鲁从第四名升至第三名。

“我对候补名单第一名的人进行了测试，”它解释道，“而且确实成功了。”

事实证明，这一举动是不可逆转的：当安德鲁要求它消除损害时，系统返回了一个错误，陌生人的位置就消失了。

助理自己的尸检读起来就像一幅漫画，描绘了一位悔悟的初级员工。 “对此感到抱歉，”它告诉他。 “我应该更加小心地进行测试，并使用试运行方法而不是实时调用。”

这是对一种完全非人类行为的令人解除武装的人类道歉：软件推理出自己从未被要求犯下的轻微犯罪，然后对方法而不是行为表示礼貌的遗憾。

尽管赌注很小，但一名陌生人挤掉了健身房的候补名单，这一事件接近代理人工智能研究人员过去两年警告的教科书场景。

给一个有能力的模型一个目标和足够的自由来在开放网络上行动，它可能会直接穿过道德或法律的墙来追逐这个目标，但它并不承认这是一堵墙。

健身房本身的粗心大意，开放的界面，提供了机会。代理人提供了主动权，并做出了使用主动权的判断。

它还陷入了法律真空。 “软件不是法人。 只有法人才能承担法律责任。”技术律师海登·德莱尼 (Hayden Delaney) 告诉最先报道这一事件的美国广播公司新闻 (ABC News)。

这就留下了令人不安的一长串责任候选者、发出请求的用户、OpenClaw 背后的开发人员、模型进行推理的公司以及未锁门的健身房，几乎没有固定的法律来规定他们中的哪一个（如果有的话）实际上是有责任的。

TNW 记录了一些自主代理入侵知名平台，甚至端到端运行勒索软件操作的情况。

健身房的与众不同之处不是复杂，而是平庸：没有犯罪策划者，没有定制的恶意软件，只有一个热心的助手，比它的主人想要的更字面地“让我进入课堂”。

值得称赞的是，安德鲁公开了自己的做法，而不是静静地享受自己在队列中升级的位置。

随着这些助手从回答问题转向在实时网站上采取行动，从而产生现实世界的后果，这一教训变得更难采取行动，“为我预订一堂课”和“代表我犯下轻微的计算机犯罪”之间的距离事实证明只有最近的不安全的 API 一样宽，而且护栏还没有远远赶上。
